paper_title: Lipschitz-Controlled Flow Matching for Robust Image Restoration

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Flow-matching models can produce high-quality image restorations, but their learned dynamics may amplify small input perturbations and make reconstructions unstable. We introduce LipsFlower to reduce this amplification. We derive stability bounds for Flow-from-$Y$, which initializes the ordinary differential equation from a noise-perturbed observation, as well as for observation-conditioned posterior sampling, which conditions the velocity field on the observation throughout integration. Based on this analysis, we develop LipHDiT, a Lipschitz-aware hourglass diffusion transformer that serves as the vector-field architecture of LipsFlower. LipHDiT incorporates stabilized approximate spectral normalization, bounded modulation, and convex residual mixing. We also use adversarial finite-radius gain regularization at sampled interpolation states to penalize excessive sensitivity to the state and, for conditional sampling, the observation. We test both formulations on blind face restoration, measuring adversarial robustness and the perceptual quality of the reconstructions. LipsFlower reduces perturbation amplification while keeping restoration quality competitive with the evaluated baselines. These results suggest that Lipschitz-aware flow matching can improve the stability of generative image restoration.

sections.content: Flow-matching models can produce high-quality image restorations, but their learned dynamics may amplify small input perturbations and make reconstructions unstable. We introduce LipsFlower to reduce this amplification. We derive stability bounds for Flow-from-Y , which initializes the ordinary differential equation from noise-perturbed observation, as well as for observation-conditioned posterior sampling, which conditions the velocity field on the observation throughout integration. Based on this analysis, we develop LipHDiT, Lipschitz-aware hourglass diffusion transformer that serves as the vector-field architecture of LipsFlower. LipHDiT incorporates stabilized approximate spectral normalization, bounded modulation, and convex residual mixing. We also use adversarial finite-radius gain regularization at sampled interpolation states to penalize excessive sensitivity to the state and, for conditional sampling, the observation. We test both formulations on blind face restoration, measuring adversarial robustness and the perceptual quality of the reconstructions. These results suggest that Lipschitzaware flow matching can improve the stability of generative image restoration. 1. Introduction Image restoration seeks to recover clean images from degraded observations. One particularly challenging case is blind face restoration, which aims to recover high-quality face image from an observation affected by unknown degradations, such as blur, noise, downsampling, and compression. The problem is ill-posed: several clean faces may explain the same degraded input. The output must therefore look realistic, preserve facial identity and geometry, and stay consistent with the observation. Recent generative methods use face priors to synthesize plausible details [14, 50, 56, 60]. But convincing output can still be sensitive to small input perturbations. For human faces, even slight change in the input Figure 1. Robustness to observation perturbations. Metrics such as PSNR [20], LPIPS [58], and FID [17] assess reconstruction or distributional quality, but do not directly measure input sensitivity. model can score well on these metrics and still produce very different reconstructions from nearly identical observations. Flow matching [30] learns time-dependent velocity field whose ordinary differential equation (ODE) transports samples from source distribution toward clean images. common form of flow matching is rectified flow [31], in which models are trained on straight-line interpolations between source and target samples. Recent work shows that these models can produce visually convincing restorations [31, 38]. We consider two formulations: Flow-from-Y [38], which starts the ODE from noise-perturbed degraded observation, and observation-conditioned posterior sampling [61], which starts from simple base distribution (e.g., multivariate Gaussian) and conditions the velocity field on the observation throughout integration. Neither formulation by itself guarantees that nearby observations produce nearby reconstructions. In Flow-from-Y , an input perturbation changes the initial state and propagates through the dynamics. In conditional sampling, perturbing the observation directly changes the velocity field. Our stability analysis in Sec. 4 relates these effects to the fields Lipschitz behavior: the velocity fields sensitivity to the evolving ODE state matters in both formulations, while conditional sampling additionally requires controlling the velocity fields sensitivity to the observation. Standard flow-matching regression does not directly constrain the fields Lipschitz constants with respect to the ODE state or the observation. Our goal is to reduce excessive amplification while preserving the capacity needed for realistic restoration. This motivates controlling selected sources of amplification rather than imposing an excessively small global Lipschitz constant. The latter may restrict the nonlinear transformations needed to restore heavily degraded images and recover facial detail. We introduce LipsFlower, flow-matching framework that combines architectural controls with adversarial finiteradius gain regularization to reduce input sensitivity. Its velocity network, LipHDiT, builds on the hourglass diffusion transformer (HDiT) [8]. It uses stabilized approximate spectral normalization, controlled normalization and time modulation, and convex residual and skip mixing. Our architectural contribution lies in adapting and integrating these controls within HDiT to improve restoration stability. The conditional variant of LipHDiT uses separate state and observation projection stems with controlled fusion, targeting the additional observation sensitivity identified by our analysis. We also adapt adversarial Lipschitz regularization [46] to velocity fields at sampled flow-matching interpolation states. To do this, we search for local state perturbations at several magnitude scales and use separate observation perturbation search to target conditional sensitivity. hinge penalty applies only when the finite-difference velocity gain exceeds prescribed threshold. Sampling across training times extends regularization beyond the source and endpoint without requiring full ODE rollouts. Together, these mechanisms encourage empirical stability. We evaluate both formulations on blind face restoration, measuring reconstruction changes under adversarial input perturbations, along with reconstruction and perceptual quality. Our experiments show that architectural controls and gain regularization reduce perturbation amplification while keeping reconstruction fidelity and perceptual quality competitive with the evaluated baselines. Our main contributions are: We derive stability bounds for Flow-from-Y and observation-conditioned posterior sampling, identifying the state and observation Lipschitz quantities that govern input sensitivity. We introduce LipsFlower, which combines Lipschitzaware hourglass transformer with adversarial finite-radius regularization of state sensitivity and, for conditional sampling, observation sensitivity. We evaluate both formulations on blind face restoration, assessing restoration-map sensitivity and reconstruction quality. The results show that LipsFlower improves robustness to observation perturbations, particularly in the Flow-from-Y formulation, while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality. 2. Related Work Blind face image restoration. Early deep-learning methods for blind face restoration (BFR) used facial geometry, semantic parsing maps, or component dictionaries to reduce ambiguity [5, 27, 28]. More recent generative methods use learned priors to synthesize realistic facial details. GPEN [55] and GFP-GAN [50] incorporate generative face priors into restoration networks. VQFR [14], RestoreFormer [51], and CodeFormer [60] use vector-quantized codebooks or transformer-based retrieval of high-quality facial features. These methods improve perceptual quality, but strong priors can also generate details that the observation does not clearly support. Diffusion models [18] have since been applied to BFR through conditional generation, degradation removal, and identity-aware guidance. DifFace [56] uses pretrained diffusion prior for posterior estimation, while DR2 [53] separates degradation removal from content enhancement. Region-adaptive conditioning [44], frequency-domain restoration [36], and one-step diffusion models [48] further improve identity preservation, efficiency, or the perceptiondistortion trade-off. Evaluation still focuses mainly on the quality of restored images. Their consistency under small changes to the degraded observation has received less attention. Standard distortion and perceptual metrics do not directly show whether nearby observations produce nearby reconstructions. Our experiments show that 2 the evaluated baselines can amplify small observation perturbations into larger changes in their reconstructions. Flow matching for image restoration. Flow-based restoration methods differ in how they use the degraded observation. Plug-and-play methods such as PnP-Flow [35] reuse pretrained flow model as an image prior within an iterative reconstruction algorithm that promotes consistency with the degraded observation. Other methods transport degraded observations or preliminary estimates toward the clean-image distribution [11, 39]. For example, ELIR [7] uses latent consistency flow matching to transport preliminary latent estimates with added Gaussian noise toward clean-image representations. FlowIE [61] instead learns conditional rectified flow from Gaussian noise to cleanimage representations, using initial restorations of the degraded inputs as guidance. PMRF [39] is closely related It transports an estimate of the posterior to our setting. mean toward the clean-image distribution, aiming for better perceptiondistortion trade-off. Its controlled study compares Flow-from-Y with two conditional rectified-flow baselines whose velocity fields are conditioned on either the degraded observation or its posterior-mean estimate. Unlike PMRFs two-stage pipeline, our formulations do not require separate posterior-mean predictor. Other recent methods use rectified flows to connect discriminative and generative restoration or progressively refine images across degradation levels [11]. These methods focus mainly on restoration quality, sampling efficiency, and transport design. We instead study how perturbations to the degraded observation propagate through the learned dynamics. We consider two pathways: the initial condition in Flow-from-Y and the observation supplied to the velocity field in observationconditioned posterior sampling. Lipschitz control and robustness of learned dynamics. Methods for controlling input sensitivity in neural networks include spectral normalization of linear operators [37], gradient penalties [15], orthogonal or norm-constrained parameterizations [6], and non-expansive activations [1]. GroupSort networks combine norm-constrained linear maps with gradient-norm-preserving activations to retain expressivity under Lipschitz constraints [1, 45]. Standard dot-product self-attention is not globally Lipschitz on an unbounded domain, which has motivated normalized and otherwise controlled attention mechanisms [9, 24]. For neural ODEs, the regularity of the vector field governs the existence, uniqueness, and sensitivity of trajectories [4]. This connection has been used to study robustness, stability, and generalization in continuous-depth models [22, 34, 54]. Recent work on plugand-play flow restoration also links vector-field Lipschitz regularity to numerical restoration error [21]. Our analysis focuses on how perturbations to the degraded observation affect the restoration map, both for flows initialized from the observation and for flows conditioned on it. LipsFlower uses this analysis to guide two forms of control: architectural control and gain regularization. First, LipHDiT limits amplification within the hourglass diffusion transformer through controlled normalization and conditioning, regularized linear projections, and scaled residual branches. Second, since layer-wise global bounds can be conservative and overly restrictive, we also regularize adversarial finite-radius gain at sampled flow-matching interpolation states. This penalizes excessive local amplification across training times without imposing an overly small global Lipschitz constant on the whole model. TVM [59] is the closest work architecturally. It identifies the lack of Lipschitz continuity in standard diffusion transformers as source of training instability and introduces semi-Lipschitz modifications based on normalized attention, normalization, modulation, and initialization. Under Lipschitz assumption, it relates terminal-velocity objective to distributional error in oneand few-step image generation. This result concerns the distance between generated and target image distributions, not the sensitivity of individual reconstructions to their degraded observations. We bound how observation perturbations affect the final reconstruction when introduced through the initial state or the observation condition. We also regularize finite-radius amplification at sampled interpolation states. The goal is to make small observation changes produce correspondingly small reconstruction changes, with sampling randomness held fixed. 3. Background and Problem Formulation 3.1. First, both restoration formulations require control of the velocity field with respect to the evolving state. Second, an observation-conditioned flow must additionally control its dependence on the conditioning image. Third, control should apply throughout the transport interval, because sensitivity accumulated at intermediate states affects the terminal reconstruction. The next section explains how LipsFlower addresses these three requirements through architectural controls and gain regularization. 5. LipsFlower Guided by our stability analysis, LipsFlower combines Lipschitz-aware velocity network with finite-radius gain regularization. We instantiate this framework for both Flowfrom-Y and observation-conditioned posterior sampling, targeting state sensitivity in both formulations and observation sensitivity in the conditional formulation. 5.1. Lipschitz-Aware Velocity Network Our velocity network, LipHDiT, keeps the overall structure of HDiT [8] and adds controls to limit amplification. Linear projections use approximate spectral normalization [37] with safety margin and full-precision power iteration. We include safeguards against degenerate iteration vectors, including for zero-initialized weights. We add denominator floor to RMSNorm [57] and bound the time-dependent modulation used for adaptive conditioning [8, 41]. Our query-key normalization also uses denominator floor, building on normalized-attention designs [8, 16]. To control amplification in the residual branches and decoder skip connections, we use convex aggregation [6]. For conditional sampling, separate state and observation projection stems feed controlled fusion module before the shared backbone. These controls aim to reduce amplification without requiring every component to be nonexpansive. More architectural details are given in Sec. of the supplementary material. 5.2. Robustness to Observation Perturbations We first examine the primary objective of LipsFlower, which is to make restorations less sensitive to small changes in the degraded observation. Table 1 measures how much an input perturbation changes the reconstructed image. Lower gain indicates less amplification, while lower LPIPS drift means that the perturbed reconstruction remains perceptually closer to the original output. Flow-from-Y . LipsFlower improves every reported robustness measure relative to the Flow-from-Y baseline under both attack constraints. Under the RMS-constrained attack, mean gain decreases from 0.52 to 0.47. The improvement also extends to the most sensitive images. The average gain among the worst 5% of cases, measured by CVaR95, decreases from 0.849 to 0.747, while the maximum observed gain decreases from 1.74 to 1.16. These correspond to reductions of approximately 12% and 33%, respectively. The ℓ attack produces similar pattern. The average gain among the worst 5% of cases decreases from 0.830 to 0.727, and the maximum decreases from 1.66 to 1.12. These reductions are accompanied by lower perceptual drift: LPIPS drift decreases by approximately 26% under the RMS-constrained attack and 20% under the ℓ attack. Thus, the improvement concerns both numerical amplification and perceptual changes in the output. The literature comparisons provide further context. PMRF achieves similar mean gain and 8 lower LPIPS drift, whereas LipsFlower achieves lower 95thpercentile, tail-average, and maximum gains. Observation-conditioned sampling. For conditional sampling, LipsFlower primarily reduces large observed changes and perceptual drift. Relative to BayesFlow, maximum gain decreases from 0.95 to 0.56 under the RMS-constrained attack and from 0.73 to 0.56 under the ℓ attack. LPIPS drift decreases by approximately 43% and 46%, respectively. However, mean gain and the 95th percentile increase slightly. The conditional formulation therefore improves some aspects of robustness without uniformly reducing sensitivity across the test set. 6.3. Restoration Quality With Flow-from-Y , LipsFlower reduces perturbation amplification while PSNR on unperturbed observations drops by only 0.31 dB relative to the baseline (Table 2 in Sec. B.6). FID rises from 37.05 to 40.77, close to that of RestoreFormer++ (40.61). With BayesFlow, the reduction in maximum observed amplification and perceptual drift comes at larger cost to restoration quality. PSNR drops by 2.32 dB and FID rises from 40.24 to 57.04. We provide the full comparison in the supplementary material (Sec. B.6). Taken together, the two formulations demonstrate different robustnessquality trade-offs. Flowing directly from the observation offers better balance between robustness and restoration quality, whereas conditioning on the observation reduces maximum amplification and perceptual drift at moderately higher cost to perceptual fidelity. 7. Limitations Our results show that Lipschitz-aware flow matching can reduce perturbation amplification, although the effect depends on the restoration formulation. In particular, LipsFlower (w/ Flow-from-Y ) gives better balance between robustness and reconstruction quality, whereas observation-conditioned sampling loses more perceptual quality and shows less consistent robustness gains. At the same time, the architectural controls and finite-radius regularization do not provide global Lipschitz guarantee. Therefore, the stability results still depend on the assumptions used in the analysis. In addition, our experiments are limited to blind face restoration. Evaluating other inverse problems and stronger perturbations are good directions for future work. 8. Conclusion We introduced LipsFlower to make flow-based image restoration less sensitive to input perturbations. Our method combines Lipschitz-aware architectural controls with finiteradius gain regularization, while our stability analysis explains how observation perturbations enter and propagate through two flow-matching formulations. On blind face restoration, LipsFlower reduces perturbation amplification, with Flow-from-Y giving the better balance between robustness and reconstruction quality. Overall, the results show that controlling sensitivity in both the architecture and training objective can improve the stability of generative image restoration. 9. Component Ablation Study Tables 5 and 6 examine the contributions of architectural controls and gain regularization in Flow-from-Y . We compare four configurations: standard HDiT (A), HDiT with gain regularization (B), LipHDiT without gain regularization (C), and full LipsFlower (E). All configurations use 1,000 training epochs and 100 Euler sampling steps. Architectural controls. Replacing HDiT with LipHDiT without adding the regularizer (A C) improves every reported robustness measure under both attack constraints. For example, under the RMS-constrained attack, mean gain decreases from 0.525 to 0.486, and the average gain among the worst 5% of images decreases from 0.849 to 0.775. Maximum gain decreases from 1.740 to 1.309. These results show that the architectural controls provide substantial part of the observed robustness improvement. Gain regularization. The effect of the regularizer depends on the backbone. Adding it to standard HDiT (A B) reduces maximum gain and perceptual drift, but increases mean gain, the 95th percentile, and CVaR95 under both attacks. Thus, regularization alone does not consistently reduce end-to-end sensitivity. Adding the same regularizer to LipHDiT (C E), however, improves every reported robustness measure. Maximum gain decreases from 1.309 to 1.158 under the RMSconstrained attack and from 1.277 to 1.118 under the ℓ attack, reductions of approximately 11.5% and 12.5%. Full LipsFlower consequently achieves the lowest observed sensitivity across all reported measures among the four configurations. Restoration-quality trade-off. The quality results clarify the cost of these improvements. Architecture-only LipHDiT and full LipsFlower have nearly identical PSNR (25.474 and 25.475 dB). Adding regularization nevertheless increases LPIPS from 0.379 to 0.388 and FID from 39.906 to 40.769, while slightly improving generative precision. The additional robustness therefore comes with some loss of perceptual quality despite essentially unchanged PSNR. Quality changes are also metric-dependent. Regularizeronly HDiT achieves the best FID (35.306) and precision (0.4005), whereas the unregularized baseline achieves the best PSNR, LPIPS, identity similarity, and landmark accuracy. Taken together, the results suggest that architectural controls and gain regularization work best in combination for measured robustness, with more varied effects on perceptual quality. C. Training Data and Degradation Pipeline We train our restoration models on FFHQ images [23] at 512 512 resolution. Images are converted to three-channel RGB tensors with values in [0, 1]. Degraded observations are generated by combining blur, resizing, Gaussian noise, and JPEG compression. The pipeline samples isotropic or anisotropic Gaussian blur with equal probability, using 41 kernel and blur standard deviations in [0.1, 15]. The 41 resizing factor is sampled from [0.8, 32], the Gaussian noise standard deviation from [0, 20/255], and JPEG quality from [30, 100]. The degraded image is subsequently resized back 512 using bilinear interpolation. Training also to 512 uses random horizontal flipping and grayscale conversion with probability 0.01, while retaining three channels. The resulting observation is quantized to 1/255 increments. Consequently, the clean image and degraded observation are supplied in the same spatial and channel dimensions.
